title: Agent vs Harness Agent vs Workflow
summary: A plain agent is one model loop with tools. A Harness Agent is the same agent pre-wired for long multi-step work. A workflow is an explicit graph where you, not the model, decide the path.
useIf: You are choosing the unit of control: model-decided path (agent or Harness) or developer-decided path (workflow).
avoidIf: A plain function can do the task. The docs say that if you can write a function, do that instead of using an agent.

explain.md: **Plain agent.** A chat client plus instructions, tools and a session. The model decides which tools to call and when to stop. Use it when the task is open-ended or one LLM call with tools is enough [[tr1]].

**Harness Agent.** Not a new runtime. `HarnessAgent` derives from `AIAgent` (.NET, `chatClient.AsHarnessAgent()`) and Python `create_harness_agent()` returns an ordinary `Agent`. It composes existing parts: function invocation with an iteration limit, per-service-call history persistence, todo tracking, plan and execute modes, session file memory, standing tool approvals, OpenTelemetry and web search where the client supports it [[tr2]]. Compaction turns on only when you give token limits or a strategy. Shared file access, background agents, shell execution and looping are opt-in.

**Workflow.** A graph of executors (agents or functions) and edges. Execution runs in supersteps with checkpoints, so order, fan-out, human gates and recovery are explicit [[tr14]]. Use it when steps are well defined or several agents must coordinate.

**They compose.** An agent can be a workflow executor, a workflow can be exposed as an agent (`workflow.as_agent()`), and a Harness Agent is an agent, so it can sit anywhere an agent can [[tr20]]. What stays your job with the Harness: session storage, telemetry exporters and the approval UX [[tr2]].

options.name: Plain function
options.summary: No model in the control path.

options.name: Harness Agent
options.summary: Agent plus todos, modes, compaction, approvals.

open.why: A function cannot plan an open-ended task.

fixed.why: Known steps are code. No tokens, no variance.

long.why: Fine, but you own state and retries.

open.why: The model chooses tools and stopping point.

fixed.why: Variance where a fixed order was enough.

long.why: No compaction, todos or per-call persistence unless you add them.

strict.why: Per-tool approval works, but queueing and standing rules are yours.

open.why: Plan and execute modes steer an open task.

fixed.why: The model still picks the path.

short.why: More defaults than the task needs.

long.why: Todos, compaction and per-call history persistence fit long runs.

none.why: Approvals are on but cost nothing if unused.

strict.why: Queued requests and standing approvals. Needs the same session each round trip.

open.why: Graphs encode known paths. Open tasks need an agent node.

strict.why: Pending requests persist in checkpoints and re-emit on restore.

explain.takeaway: Open path and long run: Harness. Known path or hard gates: workflow. Known and trivial: function.

blocks.code:
from agent_framework import Agent, create_harness_agent

plain = Agent(client=client, instructions='You are a researcher.')

harness = create_harness_agent(
    client=client,
    name='research-agent',
    max_context_window_tokens=128_000,
    max_output_tokens=16_384,   # both set: compaction on
)
session = harness.create_session()   # approvals need a session
await harness.run('Plan the migration.', session=session)

whereToUse: Plain agent: a support bot with three tools, an FAQ answerer, a classifier with one lookup
Harness Agent: research, coding, data analysis and other long-running work where the model keeps a plan and a todo list
Workflow: ETL-like pipelines with branches, regulated approvals, multi-agent hand-offs that must be auditable
Workflow containing agents: deterministic skeleton with model judgment at chosen nodes

use: Choose a plain agent when one loop with a few tools solves the task and runs finish in minutes
Choose the Harness when the run is long enough to need compaction, todos, plan/execute modes and standing approvals
Choose a workflow when order, parallelism, human gates or recovery must be explicit and testable
avoid: Do not use an agent where a function works: it adds variance, cost and latency
Do not use the Harness for a short single-tool task: defaults such as file memory and todo tools add prompt weight
Do not use a workflow for a task whose steps you cannot list in advance
flips: A compliance rule demands a fixed review order: move the control flow from the Harness into a workflow and keep agents as nodes
Runs exceed the context window: move from plain agent to Harness (or add a compaction strategy)
Approvals must survive a restart: a Harness session store may suffice, but a workflow checkpoint stores pending requests natively

pitfalls.symptom: Harness approvals never resume or ask again
pitfalls.cause: The default `ToolApprovalMiddleware` needs the same `AgentSession` across approval round trips
pitfalls.fix: Create one session per conversation, pass it every run, persist it with `to_dict()` or `SerializeSessionAsync` [[tr2]] [[tr10]]

pitfalls.symptom: Team calls the Harness "another runtime" and plans separate hosting
pitfalls.cause: It is a normal agent with pre-wired providers and middleware
pitfalls.fix: Host it like any agent; you still own session storage, exporters and the approval UI [[tr2]]

pitfalls.symptom: Workflow that wraps an agent returns only the last answer
pitfalls.cause: Orchestration terminal output became an `AgentResponse` in Python 1.2.2 (2026-04-29)
pitfalls.fix: Read `intermediate` events or `intermediate_output_from` for earlier steps [[tr49]]

scenarios.title: Overnight data research task
scenarios.situation: An analyst assistant runs 2 to 4 hours per request: it reads many files, queries tools and writes a report. A person reviews the plan before it starts. Cost per run is acceptable.
constraints: Long run, hundreds of tool calls
Plan review by a person, then autonomous execution
unknowns: Must the run survive a process restart?
Which tools change data and need approval?
How large is the context window versus the data read?
scenarios.question: Which unit do you start from?

options.name: Harness Agent in plan mode, then execute mode, with compaction limits set
options.why: Plan and execute modes model the human review, todos track progress, compaction and per-call persistence handle the long tool loop.
options.tradeoff: Looping and background agents are experimental, and you own the session store and the approval UI.

options.name: Plain agent with tools
options.why: Simple to build and fine if runs stay short.
options.tradeoff: At hundreds of tool calls you must add compaction, todo state and per-call persistence yourself.

options.name: Workflow with one node per research step
options.why: The number and order of steps are unknown, so the graph would be guesswork.
options.tradeoff: Right when the research steps are a fixed pipeline, such as fetch, extract, summarise.

flips.if: The report must be produced by a fixed sequence of reviewers
flips.then: Wrap the Harness as one node inside a workflow that fixes the review order.

flips.if: Runs are under 10 minutes with 3 tools

scenarios.takeaway: Open path plus long run points to the Harness; the graph comes when you can name the steps.

scenarios.title: Refund pipeline with audit
scenarios.situation: A refund process has intake, policy check, fraud score, manager approval and payout. Auditors want the order proven and the approval step to wait days.
unknowns: Which steps need an LLM at all?
Where do pending approvals live while waiting?
Is the host Azure Functions or containers?
scenarios.question: What do you build?

options.name: Workflow with function executors for rules and agent executors for judgment, a request port for manager approval, checkpoints in durable storage
options.why: Order is explicit, pending approval is stored in the checkpoint and re-emitted on resume, and each step is auditable.
options.tradeoff: More design effort and you must keep executor ids stable when rebuilding the graph.

options.name: Harness Agent with an approval-required payout tool
options.why: The model chooses the order, so you cannot prove the sequence, and the approval lives in session state.
options.tradeoff: Fits when the process is advisory, reversible and order does not matter.

options.name: Plain agent with a prompt that lists the steps
options.why: Prompt order is a request, not a guarantee.
options.tradeoff: Acceptable only for low-risk, reversible tasks.

flips.if: Approval waits days and you want zero idle compute
flips.then: Run the workflow on the Durable Extension.

flips.if: Only the fraud explanation needs an LLM
flips.then: Keep the pipeline as code and call one agent.

scenarios.takeaway: When order and gates must be provable, make them edges and requests, not prompts.

options: A separate runtime that replaces the agent loop
A workflow template with fixed steps
A normal agent (an `AIAgent` or `Agent`) with a pre-wired set of providers and middleware
quiz.explain: The docs state it derives from `AIAgent` in .NET and `create_harness_agent` returns an `Agent` in Python. It is not a runtime, a workflow or a host.

quiz.q: Which changes push the choice from a plain agent toward a workflow? Select all.
options: Approval must wait days and survive restarts
The path is unknown in advance
A regulator requires a provable step order
The task is a quick lookup
quiz.explain: Durable pending requests and a provable order are workflow strengths. An unknown path and quick lookups favour an agent.

flashcards.front: Which Harness defaults are on, and which are opt-in?
flashcards.back: On: function invocation limit, per-call history persistence, todos, plan/execute modes, file memory, standing approvals, OpenTelemetry. Opt-in: shared file access, background agents, shell, looping. Compaction needs token limits.

flashcards.front: Agent or workflow: who decides the next step?
flashcards.back: Agent: the model. Workflow: your graph. The docs add that if a function can do it, use the function.

flashcards.front: How do agents and workflows compose?
flashcards.back: Agents are executors in graphs, and `workflow.as_agent()` or `AsAIAgent` exposes a workflow as an agent.
